stem: A 62-year-old client who has smoked cigarettes for more than 30 years says, 'There is no point in quitting now because the cancer damage is already done.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Quitting now still lowers your risk of smoking-related cancers and other diseases; benefits occur even after many years of smoking, so cessation support is still worthwhile.
options.B: You are correct; cancer risk no longer changes once a person has smoked for several decades.
options.C: Quitting is useful only for people younger than 40 because older adults do not gain meaningful health benefit from cessation.
options.D: Continuing to smoke is reasonable if you undergo cancer screening because screening eliminates the additional cancer risk from ongoing tobacco exposure.

rationale: A is correct. CDC states that quitting smoking lowers the risk for multiple cancers and that this benefit applies regardless of age, how long a person has smoked, or how much the person has smoked. NCI likewise states that people who quit smoking, regardless of age, reduce their risk of smoking-related disease and cancer compared with people who continue to smoke. B and C are incorrect because cessation benefit is not restricted to short-term or younger smokers. D is incorrect because cancer screening does not neutralize the carcinogenic effects of continued tobacco exposure; cessation and appropriate screening address different aspects of risk and prevention.
educational_objective: Counsel a long-term older smoker that tobacco cessation remains an effective cancer-risk-reduction intervention regardless of age or smoking duration and should not be replaced by screening alone.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Health Effects of Cigarettes: Cancer; Tobacco and Cancer; Harms of Cigarette Smoking and Health Benefits of Quitting
source_version_date: CDC Health Effects of Cigarettes: Cancer updated 2024-09-17; CDC Tobacco and Cancer updated 2025-06-11; current NCI fact sheet accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: CDC 'Health Effects of Cigarettes: Cancer' — heading 'Quitting smoking can protect people from cancer', including statement that benefit applies regardless of age, smoking duration, or amount and the list of cancer-risk reductions; CDC 'Tobacco and Cancer' — 'Key points' and 'Quitting can be hard' section; NCI 'Harms of Cigarette Smoking and Health Benefits of Quitting' — questions 'What are the long-term health benefits of quitting smoking?' and 'Does quitting smoking lower the risk of getting and dying from cancer?'.
source_claim_supported: Smoking causes multiple cancers; quitting reduces cancer risk compared with continued smoking; meaningful benefit remains regardless of age and after long smoking duration.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Client Needs category 'Health Promotion and Maintenance' — prevention and/or early detection of health problems, modifiable risk reduction, health teaching and preventive counseling.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic tobacco-risk fact into a counseling scenario addressing the misconception that long-term older smokers no longer benefit from quitting. Removed unsupported cutoffs and avoided implying that screening can substitute for cessation.
audit_findings: Fresh CDC and NCI review directly supports continued cessation benefit regardless of age and smoking duration.
The final item does not promise return to never-smoker risk, specify an individual risk percentage, or impose an unsupported age cutoff.
Distractors are realistic misconceptions: irreversible risk, age-limited benefit, and screening as a substitute for cessation.
Only A is compatible with current federal cancer-prevention guidance.
Independent adversarial review found no second answer, cueing, unsupported precision, locator defect, blueprint mismatch, or unresolved conflict.
